title: A contact path for a community sports club
metaTitle: A contact path members will finish

faqs.question: What should a club contact page promise?
faqs.answer: Say who reads the message, how soon they reply in term time, and what the reply will contain. If August is slow, say so. An honest slower promise beats a fast one the rota will break.

faqs.question: How long should the first form be?
faqs.answer: Four fields is enough for a first hello: name, email or phone, which session, and an optional line. Ask for medical detail at registration, with a reason, not on the first contact. A ten-field form loses the person who was ready to play.

faqs.question: When is contact the wrong door?
faqs.answer: When half the inbox asks what time social starts, the schedule is still hidden. Put the timetable and the fees above the form, in the same words as the rest of the site. A message that remains is then a real question, which is easier to answer.

markdown:
A community sports club contact page should tell a possible member what happens after they reach out, how soon they will hear, and what to have ready. The action most people need is still to see membership or the schedule. A form with ten fields is a way to lose the ones who were ready to play.

Contact is the exception path. The schedule is the main path. Design them in that order, or the form will pretend to be the front door and then go unanswered.

## Say what happens after they send it

The page should describe the next hour of the club's side, in plain language. A person reads the message. They reply with the session that fits, or with a trial date. Fees questions go to the treasurer. Junior questions go to the junior coordinator. One destination is better than a dropdown of eight committees, if a human will route it. If nobody will route it, show the separate addresses and say which is which.

Name the inbox in human terms. "You will get a reply from the membership lead" is more reassuring than "your submission has been received," and it is only fair if it is true. If the club's habit is a reply within three days during term, say three days, and mean it. If August is slow because volunteers are away, say that August replies wait until the committee is back. An honest slower promise beats a fast promise you break.

Say what the reply will contain. A pointer to the right session. Confirmation of a trial. A note if the session is full and what the wait looks like. People can tolerate a wait when they know the shape of the answer. Silence reads as rejection.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) ask for content that is operable and understandable, including forms people can complete with assistive technology and labels that say what each field is for. A contact form with placeholder text and no labels fails that, and it fails everyone else when the placeholder disappears as they type. Put the label above the field and leave it there.

## What to have ready

Tell them the facts that let you answer in one reply. For an adult: the session they have in mind, their experience in a phrase, and a phone or email they actually check. For a parent: the child's age, the night they can travel, and any question about supervision. For a player returning from time away: the level they used to play at, stated simply.

Ask only for those facts. Experience as a paragraph, medical history, and emergency contacts belong later, at registration, with a reason. Collecting them on a first hello is how a casual enquiry starts to feel like an application to a closed squad. Some people will finish it. The ones who were on the fence will not.

If a trial requires a waiver on the night, say so, and say they can sign it there. Do not force the waiver as a PDF before you have told them which night to attend. Sequence is courtesy.

Publish a physical fallback. The hall address. The night a human is definitely there. "Come to the Tuesday social at 7 and ask for Coach Leah" is a complete contact path for people who hate forms. Many club members are those people. The website should respect them.

## Keep the form short enough to finish on a phone

Four fields is a sane default. Name. Email or phone. Which session. A message that can be one line. Mark the message optional if the session choice is enough. Required fields should be required for a reason you could say out loud.

Offer the schedule and the fees above the form, in the same words as the rest of the site. See membership or the schedule. A surprising share of "contact" visits are people who could not find the timetable. Give it to them before you ask them to write. If they still write, the message will be a real question, which is easier to answer than "what time is Tuesday."

Confirm the send on the page itself. "Message sent. Expect a reply within three days in term time." Leave them a link back to the schedule so the confirmation is not a dead end. An error should say what failed, in the club's voice, and keep what they typed.

Spam protection should be invisible or trivial. A puzzle that defeats a parent on a phone will also defeat the enquiry. If you must use a check, use one a human can pass on the first try.

## Route, reply, and the promise you printed

A published reply time is a process, not a sentence. Decide who watches the inbox, what a full session looks like in the reply, and what happens when that person is on holiday. Write the backup into the page only if it is simple. "If you have not heard within three days, write to the secretary" works when the secretary knows.

Templates help volunteers stay kind and specific. A good template names the session, attaches the fee shape, and invites them to a particular night. A bad template says "thanks for your interest in our family" and makes the visitor do the work again. Store the good template with the contact page notes so a new volunteer inherits the tone.

Do not publish a phone number that goes to a person who has asked not to receive cold calls at work. Do publish a number if a human will answer it during stated hours. "Call between 6 and 8 on club nights" is a boundary that protects the volunteer and helps the member.

Track nothing theatrical. You do not need a funnel. You need to notice if messages sit for two weeks. If they do, the page is making a promise the club's week cannot keep. Change the promise or change the rota. Leaving both in conflict will train the town to say the club never writes back.

## When contact is the wrong door

If the visitor wants to know the time, the price, or the address, the contact page is a failure of an earlier page. Fix the schedule, the fees, and the visit notes until those questions dry up. Measure dryness in the inbox, informally. When half the messages ask what time social starts, the timetable is still hidden.

Google's guidance on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether someone can leave having done the thing they came to do. On this path the thing is either a sent question with a known wait, or a realization that they did not need to write because the schedule was sitting above the form. Both are successes. A vague "get in touch" with no consequence is not.

Keep the contact item in the menu, and keep it plainly named. Contact. Membership questions. Avoid "Connect" and "Join the conversation." The club is a room with sessions, and the word should sound like that room.

Write the empty state and the full state. If a session is full, the reply should say so and should say whether a waitlist exists. If the trial night is tomorrow, the reply should say what to bring and who to ask for. Those two replies cover a large share of real messages. Draft them before you design the form, because the form is only the way those replies get triggered. A beautiful form with no reply is a suggestion box.

Keep a record of the promise on the page itself, dated, so a new volunteer can see what the website has already told people. When the promise changes, change the sentence the same day. The contact page is a public commitment. Treat it with the same care as the fee. A fee you forgot to update and a reply time you forgot to update fail in the same way: the visitor did what you asked, and the club did not do what it printed.

If the club uses a group chat for members, say so only after someone has joined, or say the rule for who gets the link. Publishing an open chat on the contact page invites strangers into a room that was meant for fixtures and apologies. The public site can point at membership. The chat can stay a benefit of membership. That boundary keeps the contact page honest about what a stranger is allowed to enter.


Print the boundary in the same size as the reply-time promise. A stranger should see, before they type, that the members' chat is a benefit of joining and that the public door is the schedule.

## What the site can live without

Once the doors work, the remaining risk is clutter that flatters the committee and confuses the member. Trophy walls, stale news, and pages that perform taste without helping someone start are the cuts. Those cuts are the subject of [what not to put on the site for a community sports club](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-community-sports-club).
